cards.title: Control What You Can
cards.insight: Stoicism teaches that external events—market crashes, job losses, others' opinions—lie beyond our control. What remains in our power is our judgment, effort, and response. By focusing energy on what we can influence, we free ourselves from the anxiety of chasing outcomes we cannot secure.
cards.takeaway: When facing uncertainty this week, identify one aspect of your situation within your control and act decisively on it.

cards.title: Virtue as the Only True Good
cards.insight: The stoics believed that living according to reason and virtue was the path to flourishing—not wealth, status, or comfort. External goods are indifferents; they have value only insofar as they support a virtuous life. This reframes success from accumulation to integrity.
cards.takeaway: Before pursuing an opportunity, ask: does this align with my values, or does it compromise my character for short-term gain?

cards.title: Prepare for Adversity
cards.insight: Stoic practice involves negative visualization—imagining hardship before it arrives. This isn't pessimism but prudent mental rehearsal that builds resilience. When difficulty comes, it feels less like a shock and more like an expected challenge to be met with calm reason.
cards.takeaway: Spend 10 minutes this week mentally preparing for one potential setback in your work or life; consider how you'd respond with composure.

cards.title: Impermanence Is Freedom
cards.insight: Everything changes—circumstances, relationships, our bodies, empires. Rather than resisting this truth, stoics embraced it as liberating. Recognizing that nothing is permanent reduces attachment to outcomes and frees us to act with urgency and wisdom in the present moment.
cards.takeaway: Reflect on one thing you're clinging to or resisting, and practice letting it go with the knowledge that change is inevitable.
